steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The closed Ruy Lopez is played the same way in thousands of master games. Why these moves, in this order, and what goes wrong when one is changed? By the end you can play the line to move 14, say what each move prepares, and name the tempting alternative that fails. Labels: [V] checked here, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis.

steps.caption: Move 5. Castling is the main choice: 10,556 of 12,714 master games from here, then 5.d3 (1,414) and 5.Nc3 (526) [V]. White leaves e4 loose on purpose. After 5...Nxe4 White hits the centre with 6.d4 or 6.Re1 and Black soon has to give the pawn back; the engine keeps White slightly better in the main Open Defence line [V], so castling does not lose a pawn. Lesson 5 plays it out.

A grab pays only if the capturer is worth less than what it takes, or if the attackers outnumber the defenders. Here a knight (3) takes a pawn (1) and a knight recaptures.

steps.text: **What 6.Re1 does.** It defends e4, so the knight cannot take it. It stands behind the pawn, so a queen that takes on e4 can be captured. And it makes the exchange on c6 followed by Nxe5 work, because e5 loses its only defender. [I] A move rarely has one job: ask what it defends, what it threatens and what it prepares.

steps.text: **What the counts can and cannot tell you.** Our master file has 329,379 games and records the first 24 half-moves, so it stops at move 12. Everything after that, here, rests on engine checks at depth 16, not on counts. A count shows what strong players chose, not which move is better: a move can be popular for fashion, preparation or style. [V]

steps.text: **Test yourself.** Six unlabelled positions follow. Each is from the main line or one move away from it. For each, ask: what does this move defend, threaten or prepare, and what does the tempting move allow? No hints are shown.

**Recap: what to remember.** The line is a chain of small purposes: castle, defend e4, kick the bishop, defend e5, prepare d4, regroup, defend e4 again. Re1 matters because it makes the exchange on c6 plus Nxe5 work. After ...b5 the pressure on c6 is gone and the bishop retreats to b3, its only good square. Without c3, d4 loses a pawn. Counts show choices, not strength.
